name: Lumberyard Apartments (Phase B)
headline: Lumberyard Apartments is the 173-unit second phase (Buildings 2 and 3) of the City of Aspen's 277-unit, permanently deed-restricted workforce rental neighborhood on city land, developed by Gorman & Company; it won CHFA's only 2026 Middle-income Housing Tax Credit award, $2,890,000 for 118 middle-income units.
why_it_matters: It shows how a resort town can stack Colorado's new middle-income credit onto a city-financed, city-owned-land deal. The city funds about $250 million from its housing fund and a voter-approved bond and keeps the land under a ground lease. APCHA joins as special limited partner for the property tax exemption. MIHTC adds about $10.5 million of equity for units at 90% to 130% AMI.

status.label: Phase A under construction; MIHTC-funded Phase B awaits closing "B" (planned May 2027)
status.detail: Closing "A" for the infrastructure and Building 1 (104 units) was completed on 2026-03-31, and the city reports construction started on 2026-04-01. The MIHTC award applies to Phase B (Buildings 2 and 3, 173 units). Phase B needs Council approval and a second financial closing, planned for May 2027, with occupancy in late 2028 and 2029.

next_step: Watch for the Aspen City Council resolution approving the closing "B" documents (planned May 2027) and the final Phase B sources and uses showing MIHTC equity, the first mortgage and Gorman funds.

key_numbers.meaning: Phase B (Buildings 2 and 3) of a 277-unit, 100% deed-restricted project. 118 units at 90% or 130% AMI carry the credit; 55 more are deed-restricted at 50%, 205% or 240% AMI.

background.text: What MIHTC is: Colorado's Middle-income Housing Tax Credit was created by House Bill 24-1316 (2024) as a five-year pilot (2025-2029). It funds rental housing for households at 80% to 120% AMI, and up to 140% AMI in rural resort counties. It is a stand-alone state credit, not paired with the federal credit, and is claimed over five years. The statutory affordability term is 15 years. CHFA may award $5M in each of 2025 and 2026 and $10M a year in 2027-2029.

Competition: CHFA's 2026 MIHTC applicant report (as of 2026-06-02) lists two applicants totaling $4,540,000, Lumberyard and an Exodus Development project in Denver. Lumberyard was the only award, for $2,890,000.

Land: the city has owned about a quarter of the site since the late 1990s, bought a large portion in 2008, and added the final piece in 2020 to assemble the roughly 11-acre site south of the Aspen Airport Business Center. The former lumberyard and mini-storage uses are named in Ordinance 10.

Site prep: in 2024-2025 the city abated asbestos in 2 structures, demolished 11 commercial buildings and removed contaminated soil (finished by end of August 2025). It applied to CDPHE's Voluntary Cleanup program and says it will be eligible for partial reimbursement through the Colorado Brownfields Tax Credit.

Process: a community design process ran from 2019 to 2022, and the land use application was filed in November 2022. Council approved entitlements on 2023-09-19 (Ordinance 10, Series of 2023: 277 units in three buildings, 435 parking spaces). The PD plan set was approved on 2025-07-02 and recorded.

Developer selection: twelve pre-qualified developers submitted proposals. Council approved a Master Development Agreement with Gorman & Company on 2025-07-14 (Resolution 100 of 2025). Gorman will build, own (leasehold) and manage the project under APCHA rules.

City investment terms (MDA): $210,000,000 of primary financing plus infrastructure expense, subject to annual appropriation, mainly as a capital contribution. Any part made as a loan would be 0% interest for at least 50 years, paid from cash flow. Where other funding programs impose restrictions (typically a 15-year compliance plus 15-year extended use), the most stringent of APCHA and CHFA/HUD rules applies.

Closing A: on 2026-03-24 Council adopted Resolution 042, Series of 2026, approving the deed restriction, ground lease, operating agreement, development services agreement, APCHA special limited partner addendum and construction license. APCHA's board approved the SLP agreement on 2026-03-18. Closing A was completed on 2026-03-31.
APCHA as special limited partner lets the project qualify for property tax exemption and certain sales tax benefits, lowering operating costs. APCHA has no day-to-day management role.

Cost: the whole project was estimated at $360M in November 2025 (about $1.3M per unit including roads, utilities, underground parking, a transit station and a trail underpass). Gorman agreed to raise about $110M from outside sources and invest about $7M of its own.

Design changes for Building 1 (within PD flexibility): 7% less gross floor area, optimized for double-loaded modular, elevators cut from 4 to 2, and sound walls replaced with trees after CDOT rejected them in its right-of-way.

What the MIHTC levels mean in Pitkin County (CHFA 2026 limits, rural resort county). At 90% AMI: maximum rent $2,398 (1BR), $2,877 (2BR), $3,325 (3BR); income limit $89,550 (1 person), $127,890 (4 people). At 130% AMI: $3,464, $4,156 and $4,803; $129,350 and $184,730. Actual rents follow APCHA rent categories and are not published in the records I found.

discrepancies: MIHTC column: CHFA's award report heads the $2,890,000 column "MIHTC Amount Requested"; CHFA's award description page says "MIHTC Awarded: $2,890,000". The figures match. [chfa-mihtc-award; chfa-mihtc-desc]
Building 1 size: the Aspen Times (2026-03-11) reported a 109-unit first building; the city's staff reports and sources-and-uses say 104 units. [at-2026-03-11; aspen-res042; aspen-sources-uses]

Closing A city funds: the 2026-03-16 staff report labels $39,948,000 as "City Phase 0 Funds" and $78,844,765 as "City Phase 1 Funds". The city's post-closing summary assigns $78,844,765 to infrastructure and $39,948,000 to Building #1. [aspen-res042; aspen-sources-uses]

Closing A first mortgage: $15,700,000 in the March staff reports versus $10,700,000 (plus $12,053,163 other sources) in the April 2026 post-closing summary; both total $22,753,163 of non-city sources. [aspen-res042; aspen-mar9; aspen-sources-uses]
Income range: the city's project page says "below 50% AMI up to 240% AMI"; Gorman's release and CHFA's Phase B mix say 50% to 240%. [aspen-lumberyard-page; gorman-pr-2026-04; chfa-mihtc-desc]
Site area: "11-acre" (Gorman, city) versus 11.3 acres (Aspen Times, quoting the city's project manager). [gorman-pr-2026-04; at-2025-11-17]

Construction start: the city page says construction started 2026-04-01; Gorman's March schedule put Phase 0 mobilization in April/May 2026 and the Building 1 vertical start in September 2026. [aspen-lumberyard-page; aspen-mar9]
open_questions: Phase B final budget: first mortgage, MIHTC equity investor and price, Gorman funds and developer fee are TBD until closing B.
Whether $2,890,000 is the annual or the total MIHTC amount is not stated outright. The city's $10.5M equity estimate implies an annual figure (inference).
Actual rents and APCHA rent categories for each AMI tier are not published in the records reviewed.
The Phase B owner entity (presumably a Lumberyard Apartments 2/3, LLC) and the city's percentage interest in it are not public.
The Employer Partnership Program terms (share of units, pricing) were still being set; a Council work session was set for 2026-11-02.
Whether the Colorado Brownfields Tax Credit reimbursement has been received is not public.
The share of the $78.8M closing A infrastructure spend that serves Phase B is not broken out in the city summaries.
